auxiliary_material: The authors noted that in vitro experiments used inosine concentrations of 10mM to 30mM, which they acknowledged exceed physiological serum levels, highlighting a gap between experimental conditions and in vivo reality. The study design excluded patients with recent antibiotic use to minimize microbiome perturbation. Statistical associations were adjusted for clinical covariates like age and ferritin. The authors explicitly stated limitations regarding sample size, the observational design restricting causal inference, and the use of hematologic malignancy models which differ from solid tumors.
outline_action: Continue searching for clinical studies specifically involving solid tumor cohorts (e.g., melanoma, NSCLC) treated with PD-1/PD-L1 inhibitors that publish quantitative metabolomics data including absolute serum or TME concentrations of inosine and SCFAs. When evaluating potential sources, verify if numerical concentration data is present in the text or tables, not just in unretrieved figures. Use the mechanistic findings from this study (A2A receptor modulation by inosine) to frame the biological plausibility section of the review, while clearly distinguishing the CAR T/lymphoma context from the ICI/solid tumor gap.
remaining_gap: The specific success criteria require absolute concentration values (μM/ng/mL) of inosine and SCFAs in human solid tumor patients treated with immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICI), with statistical association to ORR/PFS. This study does not meet these criteria because: (1) the cohort consists of lymphoma patients receiving CAR T-cell therapy, not solid tumor patients receiving ICI; (2) the supplied text reports statistical significance and hazard ratios for serum inosine but does not explicitly state the absolute concentration values (e.g., mean/median μM) in the text body; (3) SCFA associations were reported primarily with adverse events rather than direct efficacy endpoints like ORR/PFS in this text; (4) the tumor microenvironment (TME) concentrations were not measured, only serum.
useful_material: This study prospectively analyzed 47 patients with relapsed/refractory diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (R/R-DLBCL) receiving CD19 CAR T-cell therapy. It quantified serum inosine and short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs: acetate, butyrate, isovalerate) using liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry. The authors reported that responders had significantly higher pretreatment serum inosine levels compared to non-responders (P = .042), and submedian serum inosine was an independent predictor of shorter progression-free survival (Multivariate HR 2.78, P = .024). For SCFAs, higher serum acetate and butyrate were associated with the absence of adverse events (CRS/ICANS), while elevated isovalerate was linked to the presence of adverse events. The study also identified an enrichment of inosine biosynthesis pathways in the gut microbiome of responders and demonstrated in vitro that inosine could enhance CAR T-cell cytotoxicity via the adenosine A2A receptor.
